notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Proverbs 8, drawn from the sources accessible through the permitted sites.

---

## Overview of the Chapter

The Pulpit Commentary divides the chapter into four sections: (1) Wisdom’s public call and the reasons to trust her (vv. 1–11); (2) Wisdom displays her excellence (vv. 12–21); (3) Wisdom discourses on her origin and role in creation (vv. 22–31); (4) Wisdom renews her appeal to be heard (vv. 32–36). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/8.htm)

Gill reads the entire chapter Christologically: "Christ, under the name of Wisdom, is represented as an herald, publishing the Gospel in the ministry of the word." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/8.htm)

---

## Verses 1–3: Wisdom’s Public Call

**v. 1: "Does not wisdom call out, and understanding raise her voice?"**

The rhetorical question expects a "yes." Ellicott notes the contrast with the secret allurements of the immoral woman in chapter 7 — Wisdom speaks openly, not in corners. He compares John 18:20: "I spake openly to the world… and in secret have I said nothing." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/8.htm)

Gill identifies "Wisdom" as Christ, the Wisdom of God, whose "crying" signifies "proclaiming, publishing, preaching the everlasting Gospel." The contrast is between the herald at noon-day and "the whispers of a harlot, at night, in a corner." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/8.htm)

Guzik (Enduring Word) notes that wisdom is personified as "a noble, beautiful, helpful woman in contrast to the immoral woman described in Proverbs 7." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-8/)

The Pulpit Commentary adds: "The open, bold, and public utterances of Wisdom are in happy contrast to the secret and stealthy enticements of Vice." It also notes that we, reading by the light of later revelation, "see in the description of Wisdom no mere ideal of practical prudence… but an adumbration of him who is the Wisdom of God, the coeternal Son of the Father." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/8.htm)

**v. 2: "On the heights overlooking the road, at the crossroads she takes her stand."**

Gill explains that Wisdom chooses high places "to be both seen and heard, for which reason Christ went up into a mountain and preached" (Matthew 5:1). At the crossroads she stands "where more ways than one met together, and so difficult to know which was the right path to take; here Christ stands in the ministry of the word to direct." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/8.htm)

Guzik quotes Kidner: "A chapter which is to soar beyond time and space, opens at street-level, to make it clear, first, that the wisdom of God is as relevant to the shopping-centre (Proverbs 8:2-3) as to heaven itself (Proverbs 8:22)." He also quotes Garrett: "Wisdom is for ordinary people—she is not confined to the academic classroom or to sacred precincts of the temple. Nor is she high atop some mountain where only the hardiest and most determined will find her." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-8/)

The Pulpit Commentary: "She takes her stand, not in thievish corners of the streets, like the harlot, but in the most open and elevated parts of the city, where she may be best seen and heard by all." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/8.htm)

**v. 3: "Beside the gates to the city, at the entrances she cries out."**

Ellicott notes the city gates were where courts of judgment met and where people continually passed. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/8.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary: "She posts herself at the side of the city gates, under the archway pierced in the wall, where she is sure of an audience… It is a fine picture of the comprehensiveness of the gospel, which is meant for high and low, prince and peasant." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/8.htm)

---

## Verses 4–11: Wisdom’s Appeal and the Worth of Her Words

**v. 4: "To you, O men, I call out, and my cry is to the sons of men."**

Ellicott notes a distinction in the Hebrew: "O men" (ishim) means "great ones"; "sons of man" (bene adam) refers to those of inferior rank. Thus Wisdom calls to all classes without distinction. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/8.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary likewise explains that ishim are "men in the highest sense, who have some wisdom and experience," while bene adam are "children of Adam," the general mass "taken up with material interests." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/8.htm)

Gill sees the call as going to all humanity without distinction: "Not angels, the fallen angels… nor the brutes, irrational creatures… but 'men', whom God has loved and Christ has redeemed." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/8.htm)

**v. 5: "O simple ones, learn to be shrewd; O fools, gain understanding."**

The "simple" (pethaim) are those not yet perverted but easily influenced either way. The Pulpit Commentary explains the word for "shrewd" (ormah) is used here in a good sense — "subtlety" or practical wisdom (calliditas). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/8.htm)

Gill: "They are 'the simple' who are weak and easy to be imposed upon, who are here called unto; and generally speaking such are they to whom the mysteries of grace are made known, while they are hid from the wise and prudent." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/8.htm)

**v. 6: "Listen, for I speak of noble things, and the opening of my lips will reveal right."**

The Hebrew word nagid usually means "prince" or "leader," so the Pulpit Commentary renders it "princely" or "noble" things — fitting for Wisdom's discourse. The Vulgate has de rebus magnis ("of great things"). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/8.htm)

Gill: "Or 'princely things,' as the word may be rendered; which became him who is the Prince of the kings of the earth… to speak; and are worthy to be received by princes." He adds that they are "principal" or "leading" truths of greatest importance. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/8.htm)

**v. 7: "For my mouth will speak the truth, and wickedness is detestable to my lips."**

Gill notes: "Wisdom, or Christ… is truth itself; nothing else can come out of his mouth." He identifies the particular "wickedness" as "the sin of lying more especially, as opposed to truth." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/8.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary: The Hebrew verb hagah for "speak" properly means "to meditate" or "speak with oneself," but joined with "palate" (chek) it must signify "to utter." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/8.htm)

**v. 8: "All the words of my mouth are righteous; none are crooked or perverse."**

Ellicott: "Froward — That is, twisted, or crooked." Wisdom's words contain no distortion of truth. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/8.htm)

Gill: The words are "concerning righteousness" — the necessity of righteousness for eternal life, the insufficiency of man's own righteousness, the excellency of Christ's righteousness. "There is nothing froward or perverse in them… nor is there any contradiction in the doctrines of the Gospel one to another." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/8.htm)

**v. 9: "They are all plain to the discerning, and upright to those who find knowledge."**

Ellicott explains the words are plain only to the spiritual man, citing 1 Corinthians 2:10, 14: the "natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/8.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary: "Opening his heart to receive Divine instruction, he is rewarded by having his understanding enlightened." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/8.htm)

Guzik: "There is clarity and a straightforward character to wisdom, one that contrasts with elaborate so-called hidden truths and mysteries." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-8/)

**v. 10: "Receive my instruction instead of silver, and knowledge rather than pure gold."**

Gill explains: "Not but that silver may be desired… but when they are in competition, the one is to be preferred to the other." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/8.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary notes the comparison is implied in the first clause and made explicit in the second — similar to Hosea 6:6 ("I desired mercy, and not sacrifice"). The inferior thing is not necessarily of no value, but always of lesser importance. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/8.htm)

**v. 11: "For wisdom is more precious than rubies, and nothing you desire compares with her."**

See Proverbs 3:14–15 for the same sentiment. The Pulpit Commentary and Ellicott both cross-reference that earlier passage. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/8.htm)

Guzik: "Without wisdom, one may have the riches of this world and a miserable life. Early in his reign Solomon desired wisdom above all riches and was greatly blessed because of it (1 Kings 3:10-13)." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-8/)

---

## Verses 12–21: What Wisdom Has and What Wisdom Gives

**v. 12: "I, wisdom, dwell together with prudence, and I find knowledge and discretion."**

The Pulpit Commentary renders this: "I have made subtilty my dwelling." Wisdom inhabits prudence, animating it. The Septuagint has "I wisdom dwelt (κατεσκήνωσα) in counsel and knowledge," which the Pulpit Commentary notes recalls John 1:14: "The Word was made flesh, and dwelt (ἐσκήνωσεν) among us." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/8.htm)

Ellicott: "Dwell with prudence — literally, inhabit it, have settled down and taken up my abode with it, am at home there." The "witty inventions" (mezimmoth) are "well thought out plans," the same word translated "discretion" in Proverbs 1:4. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/8.htm)

Guzik quotes Clarke: "Prudence is defined, wisdom applied to practice; so wherever true wisdom is, it will lead to action." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-8/)

**v. 13: "To fear the LORD is to hate evil; I hate arrogant pride, evil conduct, and perverse speech."**

The Pulpit Commentary notes Wisdom here "enunciates the proposition which is the foundation of all her teaching," but "on the reverse side" — not as the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 1:7; 9:10) but as the hatred of evil. "There can be no fellowship between light and darkness; he who serves the Lord must renounce the works of the devil." Pride and arrogance are listed first "which are opposed to the sovereign virtue of humility." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/8.htm)

Gill emphasizes that this filial fear "is consistent with strong faith, great joy, and true courage." He notes that pride appears "in men in thinking too highly of themselves… in setting up and trusting to their own righteousness for salvation," which Christ must hate. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/8.htm)

Ellicott: "Because there can never be any truce between the kingdoms of light and darkness (Matthew 6:24), so if we are the friend of one, we must be the enemy of the other." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/8.htm)

**v. 14: "Counsel and sound judgment are mine; I have insight and strength."**

The Pulpit Commentary discusses the word tushiyyah ("sound wisdom"): it occurs mainly in Job and Proverbs, meaning "elevation," "furtherance," or "substance" — "that which is essentially good and useful." Wisdom does not merely possess these attributes; "they are her very nature." It notes an echo of Isaiah 11:2 (the seven gifts of the Spirit) and Isaiah 9:6 ("Wonderful, Counsellor, the Mighty God"). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/8.htm)

Ellicott compares Ecclesiastes 7:19 and the gifts listed in Isaiah 11:2. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/8.htm)

**v. 15–16: "By me kings reign, and rulers enact just laws; By me princes rule, and all nobles who govern justly."**

The Pulpit Commentary: "By possession of wisdom kings are enabled to discharge their functions duly and righteously. So Solomon prayed for wisdom to enable him to rule his subjects properly (1 Kings 3:9)." The word for "princes" (rozenim) means "those who weigh causes." "Decree justice" is literally "to engrave just decrees on tablets." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/8.htm)

Ellicott: "By the aid of heavenly wisdom only can they give right and just judgments, and so fulfil the high office delegated to them by God Himself, from the possession of which they are themselves termed 'gods' (Exodus 22:28; Psalm 82:1)." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/8.htm)

Guzik: "Many gain power, stay in power, and exercise power through gaining and using wisdom." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-8/)

**v. 17: "I love those who love me, and those who seek me early shall find me."**

Ellicott compares John 14:21: "He that loveth me… I will love him." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/8.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary: "Love attracts love. 'Magnes amoris est amor.' They who love virtue and wisdom are regarded with favour by God." It notes the Septuagint changes the verbs (Ἐγὼ τοὺς ἐμὲ φιλοῦντας ἀγαπῶ), reminiscent of the interchange of ἀγαπάω and φιλέω in John 21:15–17. "Those that seek me early" means "earnestly" or "strenuously" — "as people deeply interested in any pursuit rise betimes to set about the necessary work." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/8.htm)

**v. 18–19: "With me are riches and honor, enduring wealth and righteousness. My fruit is better than gold…"**

Ellicott warns against reading this in a purely material sense: "If this passage is taken in a material sense, Psalm 112:3 and the promises in the Pentateuch of wealth as the reward of obedience might be compared with it. But doubtless the 'true riches' (Luke 16:11) are here alluded to, the consciousness of possessing God's honour and favour, called in Ephesians 3:8 the 'unsearchable riches of Christ.'" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/8.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary: "Durable, עָתֵק (athek), occurs only here… and means 'old,' 'venerable,' 'long accumulated;' hence firm and lasting. Righteousness is the last reward that Wisdom bestows, without which, indeed, all material blessings would be nothing worth." It adds a Christian caveat: "We Christians, however, look not for reward in uncertain riches, but in God's favour here and happiness in another world." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/8.htm)

**v. 20: "I walk in the way of righteousness, along the paths of justice."**

The Pulpit Commentary: "I swerve not to one side or the other (Proverbs 4:27)." It compares the promise of Isaiah 30:21: "Thine ears shall hear a word behind thee, saying, This is the way, walk ye in it." Aristotle's idea that virtue is the mean between two extremes is invoked. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/8.htm)

**v. 21: "bestowing wealth on those who love me and making their treasuries full."**

Ellicott spiritualises the wealth: "The work which each one by my help shall do will be stored up for him in heaven (Matthew 6:20), it will be as 'gold tried in the fire' (Revelation 3:18)." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/8.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary: The word for "substance" (yesh) means "real, valuable possessions." This refers to "treasure in heaven… bags which wax not old… an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away" (Matthew 6:20; Luke 12:33; 1 Peter 1:4). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/8.htm)

---

## Verses 22–31: Wisdom's Origin and Role in Creation

**This is the most debated section in the chapter, especially v. 22, because of its role in the Arian controversy of the 4th century.**

**v. 22: "The LORD created me as His first course, before His works of old." (BSB) / "The LORD possessed me at the beginning of his way" (KJV)**

The Hebrew verb is *qanah*. This is the crux of a major interpretive divide:

- **Translation debate:** Ellicott explains that *qanah* originally signified "to set up" or "establish," and is applied to (1) "forming" the heavens (Genesis 14:19), (2) "begetting" a son (Deuteronomy 32:6), (3) "acquiring" (Genesis 4:1), (4) "purchasing" (Genesis 25:10), and (5) "owning" (Isaiah 1:3). Since "set up" and "brought forth" are used as synonyms just after, Ellicott concludes the sense is that Wisdom was "formed" or "begotten" before Creation. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/8.htm)

- Guzik (Enduring Word) argues that "on balance the best translation is **possessed**." He details the Arian controversy: "Arius used this verse from the Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures, which puts the phrase like this: *The Lord created me at the beginning of His way*. Arius argued that Jesus is the wisdom of God, and this verse spoke of His creation. If Jesus was created, then He had a beginning and was not eternal, and if not eternal, then not God." Guzik rejects this, saying that while Jesus is the wisdom of God, "the woman of Proverbs 8 does not directly describe Jesus" in a one-to-one correlation. He also notes "the verb *qanah* can mean either 'possess' or 'create.' The older versions chose 'possess'; otherwise it might sound as if God lacked wisdom and so created it before the world began." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-8/)

- **Gill (Baptist) reads it Christologically:** "Not 'created me', as the Targum and the Septuagint version; which version Arius following gave birth to his pernicious doctrine." Gill insists "the Word, or Wisdom of God is never said to be created; and if as such he was created, God must have been without his Wisdom before he was created; besides, Christ, as the Word and Wisdom of God, is the Creator of all things, and not created." He translates it as "the LORD begat me" (comparing Zechariah 13:5 in the Septuagint) and explains it as denoting "the Lord's having, possessing, and enjoying his word and wisdom as his own proper Son." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/8.htm)

- **Athanasius (Church Father, as cited by LCMS and TGC):** The Lutheran Witness notes that both Athanasius and the Arians "assumed" Wisdom in Proverbs 8 is Christ (based on 1 Corinthians 1:24). But Athanasius argued that Proverbs must be interpreted figuratively, "latently." He contended that "created" refers not to Christ's eternal essence but to His incarnation — "My Father hath prepared for Me a body, and has created Me for men in behalf of their salvation." (https://witness.lcms.org/2021/parsing-the-proverbs-with-st-athanasius/) The same point appears in Athanasius's writings via BibleHub: "What is created is not Wisdom per se, but the body given at the incarnation." (https://www.biblehub.com/library/athanasius/select_works_and_letters_or_athanasius/chapter_xix_texts_explained_sixthly.htm)

- **The Gospel Coalition (Reformed/Baptist):** Matt Emerson writes that "almost everyone agreed that Lady Wisdom is a figurative depiction of God the Son" in the early church because "other biblical texts identify Jesus as God's Wisdom, most importantly 1 Corinthians 1:24." He argues Proverbs 8:22–31 teaches the eternal generation of the Son: "God's Wisdom—God the Son—is from God the Father… God the Son is brought forth by God the Father (Prov. 8:25)—or, to use the technical terminology of the Nicene Creed, God the Son is eternally begotten of God the Father. Of course this doesn't mean… the Son was created in time." (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/jesus-proverbs/)

- **Catholic reading (Haydock):** "Possessed. As Christ was with God, equal to him in eternity, John i. Septuagint, 'created,' which many of the Fathers explain of the word incarnate." Haydock notes the Septuagint generally renders *qanah* as "possessed," as Aquila does here. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/proverbs-8.html)

- **Peake's Commentary (modern scholarship, via StudyLight):** Takes a different approach: "Wisdom is not conceived as eternally coexistent with God, but as formed before Creation to be the instrument of creation. Cf. the Rabbinical doctrine that the Law was created before the world, and the Philonian conception of the Logos." It renders v. 22a: "the LORD formed me as the first (or chief) of His ways." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/proverbs-8.html)

**v. 23: "From everlasting I was established, from the beginning, before the earth began."**

Ellicott notes the unusual Hebrew verb nasak ("set up" / "established") is "also applied to our Lord in Psalm 2:6 when 'set' as King on Zion." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/8.htm)

Haydock's Catholic Commentary notes: "Hebrew, 'anointed.' Septuagint, 'he founded.' Christ was appointed to be the foundation, on which we must be built. (St. Athanasius iii. Orat.)" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/proverbs-8.html)

**v. 24–25: "When there were no watery depths, I was brought forth… Before the mountains were settled, before the hills, I was brought forth."**

Gill interprets "brought forth" (cholalti) as referring to eternal generation: "the word חוללתי is used of generation… Christ is the firstborn of every creature, begotten, born, and brought forth before any creature was in being." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/8.htm)

Ellicott: "I was brought forth — i.e., born. The same word is used in Psalm 51:5 (7), and Job 15:7." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/8.htm)

**v. 27–29: "I was there when He established the heavens, when He inscribed a circle on the face of the deep…"**

These verses poetically recount creation. Ellicott explains "set a compass" (v. 27) refers to stretching "the vault of heaven over" the deep — the same expression used in Job 22:14. For v. 29, he compares the same thoughts in Job 38:4, 10–11. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/8.htm)

**v. 30: "Then I was a skilled craftsman at His side, and His delight day by day, rejoicing always in His presence."**

Ellicott discusses the word translated "skilled craftsman" (amon): "As one brought up with him — i.e., his foster child; as Mordecai 'brought up' Esther (Esther 2:7). But the word may also bear the sense of 'artificer.'… This meaning is much more suitable, and harmonises with Psalm 104:24; Psalm 136:5, and Hebrews 1:2." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/8.htm)

The Gospel Coalition: "The term translated 'master workman' (v. 30) means something like 'architect.' In his eternal divinity, God the Son (i.e. Wisdom) is the 'master workman' at the Father's side, the architect of creation." (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/jesus-proverbs/)

Guzik: "God used wisdom and intelligence in the design of the universe. If we represent wisdom as a person, then it can be said that wisdom was with God in creation… I was beside Him as a master craftsman." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-8/)

Ellicott also notes on "I was daily his delight": "The pronoun 'his' does not occur in the Hebrew, which is, literally, I was delights, i.e., all joy, delight, as Psalm 109:4: 'I am prayer,' i.e., give myself wholly to it." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/8.htm)

**v. 31: "I was rejoicing in His whole world, delighting together in the sons of men."**

Ellicott: "Rather, the fertile part. (Comp. Genesis 1:31, where the satisfaction of God with His creation is described; and Psalm 104:31.)" On "my delights were with the sons of men," he adds: "Such appearances as this, and that to Abraham in Genesis 18, and to Joshua in Joshua 5, were supposed by the Fathers to have been anticipations of the Incarnation of God the Son, who is here described under the name of Wisdom." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/8.htm)

Gill speaks of "Christ's wonderful delight and pleasure in the sons of men." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/8.htm)

---

## Verses 32–36: Final Appeal and Warning

**v. 32: "Now therefore, my sons, listen to me, for blessed are those who keep my ways."**

Ellicott: "Now that ye know how great my power is, and what love I have to you, in that I rejoice in you, and call you my sons. (Comp. 1 John 3:1.)" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/8.htm)

Guzik: "Having given her impressive résumé, now wisdom can make a reasoned appeal that we listen to her." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-8/)

**v. 33: "Listen to instruction and be wise; do not ignore it."**

Guzik: "Given that wisdom has proven herself to be good and reliable, and that she brings many blessings with her, we should give wisdom our attention and never disdain it." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-8/)

**v. 34: "Blessed is the man who listens to me, watching daily at my gates, waiting at the posts of my doorway."**

Ellicott: "A figure taken from an ardent scholar waiting till the doors of the school are opened, and he can begin his studies. Or it represents a courtier expecting the appearance of his sovereign, or a lover that of his mistress. (Comp. Wisdom Of Solomon 8:2.)" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/8.htm)

Guzik quotes Clarke: "Wisdom is represented as having a school for the instruction of men; and seems to point out some of the most forward of her scholars coming, through their intense desire to learn, even before the gates were opened, and waiting there for admission, that they might hear every word that was uttered, and not lose one accent of the heavenly teaching. Blessed are such." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-8/)

**v. 35: "For whoever finds me finds life and obtains the favor of the LORD."**

Ellicott: "Comp. 1 John 5:12; John 8:51; and above, Proverbs 3:18, where Wisdom is described as a 'tree of life.'" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/8.htm)

Guzik quotes Trapp on "obtains favor from the LORD": "Which is better than life. God's favour is no empty favour; it is not like the winter's sun, that casts a goodly countenance when it shines, but gives little heat or comfort." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-8/)

**v. 36: "But he who fails to find me harms himself; all who hate me love death."**

Ellicott notes on "sinneth against me": "Rather, He that misses me does not find me. So in Greek, sin (ἁμαρτία) is a 'missing' of the true object of life." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/8.htm)

Guzik quotes Poole: "'Love death' — 'Not directly or intentionally, but by consequence, because they love those practices which they know will bring certain destruction upon them.'" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-8/)

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### The Christological Reading of vv. 22–31

- **Reformed / Gospel Coalition (Baptist-influenced):** Tends to read Proverbs 8 Christologically, connecting Lady Wisdom to 1 Corinthians 1:24. The eternal generation of the Son is seen in the language of being "brought forth." (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/jesus-proverbs/)

- **Desiring God (Baptist/Reformed):** More cautious. The article notes that "numerous proponents of preaching Christ from the Old Testament acknowledge that although this passage may foreshadow the role of Christ as the wisdom of God… it is better viewed as a poetic personification of wisdom." It quotes Richard Belcher: "It is difficult from an OT standpoint to argue that Lady Wisdom in Proverbs 8 is a divine hypostasis of Christ's eternal divine nature." (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/how-to-preach-proverbs)

- **Enduring Word (Guzik, broadly charismatic/evangelical):** Argues clearly that the woman of Proverbs 8 "does not directly describe Jesus." He says: "Because Jesus is God, He has and expresses and demonstrates the wisdom of God; but the woman of Proverbs 8 does not directly describe Jesus." The key error of Arius, according to Guzik, was over-reading the correlation and mistranslating *qanah*. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-8/)

- **Gill (older Baptist):** Reads the entire chapter Christologically without reservation: "Christ, under the name of Wisdom." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/8.htm)

- **Lutheran (LCMS):** Holds with Athanasius that Wisdom in Proverbs 8 is Christ. The Lutheran Witness article states: "They were convinced from the text itself that this Wisdom is Christ Himself, as St. Paul says, 'Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God' (1 Cor. 1:24)." The Hebrew *qanah* "is much clearer and is rightly translated, 'possess.'" (https://witness.lcms.org/2021/parsing-the-proverbs-with-st-athanasius/)

### Material vs. Spiritual Riches (vv. 18–21)

- **Ellicott (Anglican) and Pulpit Commentary:** Both lean strongly toward spiritualising "riches and honour" — reading them as the true riches of Christ, treasure in heaven, and the consciousness of God's favour. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/8.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/8.htm)

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Takes a more balanced view: "Those who love and pursue wisdom will find themselves rewarded. They will find wisdom… and the blessings wisdom brings (riches and honor… righteousness). It could even be said that wisdom seeks out her followers to bless them (that I may cause those who love me to inherit wealth)." Guzik does not explicitly spiritualise the material promises, though he also does not press a prosperity-gospel reading. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-8/)

## Other Views

### Catholic and Orthodox Readings

- **Catholic (Haydock, via StudyLight):** On v. 22, Haydock notes that "Possessed" is the correct reading ("As Christ was with God, equal to him in eternity"). He acknowledges the Septuagint reads "created," which "many of the Fathers explain of the word incarnate." On v. 23, he notes the Hebrew can mean "anointed" and the Septuagint has "founded" — "Christ was appointed to be the foundation, on which we must be built. (St. Athanasius iii. Orat.)" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/proverbs-8.html)

- **Orthodox (OCA.org):** No specific material was found from oca.org in the search results.

- **Athanasius (Church Father, shared heritage of Catholic and Orthodox):** Argues that Proverbs must be read as "proverbs" (figurative language), not "nakedly in their first sense." The "creation" of Wisdom in v. 22 refers to the incarnation — the body prepared for Christ — not to the eternal Son's essence. (https://www.biblehub.com/library/athanasius/select_works_and_letters_or_athanasius/chapter_xix_texts_explained_sixthly.htm)

### Modern Scholarship

- **Peake's Commentary (via StudyLight):** Treats Wisdom as "not conceived as eternally coexistent with God, but as formed before Creation to be the instrument of creation." It compares this to "the Rabbinical doctrine that the Law was created before the world, and the Philonian conception of the Logos as first immanent, and then for creation… emanating from God in a quasi-personal form of existence." It also notes: "In Ecclus. the conception of Wisdom found here is identified with the Torah." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/proverbs-8.html)

## Summary of Key Debated Points

1. **The identity of Lady Wisdom:** Is she merely a poetic personification, or is she a direct portrayal of the pre-incarnate Christ? The early church, Gill, LCMS Lutherans, and TGC broadly read her Christologically. Guzik (Enduring Word) and some at Desiring God caution against a direct one-to-one equation, preferring to see her as a personification that foreshadows Christ.

2. **The translation of *qanah* in v. 22:** "Possessed" (KJV, older versions, Gill, Guzik, LCMS) vs. "created" (LXX, BSB) vs. "formed/begot" (Ellicott, Peake). This was the flashpoint of the Arian controversy.

3. **The nature of the promised riches (vv. 18–21):** Spiritual (Ellicott, Pulpit) vs. both spiritual and material (Guzik, perhaps).
